---
title: "08 – RQ2 & RQ3: Windowed Cross-Recurrence Analysis"
format: html
editor: visual
---

# Overview

**RQ2** – Do emotion words co-occur across conversational turns (child ↔ partner)? **RQ3** – Is there a directional influence in emotion word use between child and partner?

**Method: Windowed Cross-Recurrence Rate (wRR)**

We build a cross-recurrence plot (CRP) for each transcript — an N×N binary matrix where cell (i, j) = 1 if child's i-th turn and partner's j-th turn both contain ≥1 emotion word, and 0 otherwise. Only (1,1) entries are marked as recurrent: matching zeros (both speakers silent) carry no information about emotional coupling.

We restrict attention to a **diagonal band** of width ±W around the main diagonal (all cells where \|i−j\| ≤ W). This band captures lagged co-occurrence up to W turns away, while excluding distant, temporally irrelevant pairings.

**Windowed Recurrence Rate (wRR)** = recurrent points in band / total cells in band.

**Directionality** — above vs. below the diagonal carries directional meaning:

- lag L = j − i \> 0 (above diagonal): child uses emotion at turn i, partner at later turn j → **child leads**
- lag L = j − i \<= 0 (below diagonal): partner speaks first → **partner leads**

Asymmetry index = RR at positive lags − RR at negative lags (positive = child leads).

**Window size W** is chosen from the data's own inter-event interval (IEI) distribution (see Section 5).

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 0. Setup

```{r setup, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
source("00_setup.R")
library(lme4)
library(lmerTest)   # Satterthwaite p-values for lmer fixed effects
library(splines)
library(emmeans)
library(broom.mixed)
library(ggeffects)
library(dplyr)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 1. Load data

```{r load-data}
utt <- readRDS(here("01Data", "02Derived", "FINAL_utt_RQ1_emotions_merged.rds"))

# Apply the same corpus exclusions as 02Demographics.qmd and 07RQ1DataAnalysis.qmd
EXCLUDE_CORPORA <- c("Feldman", "Peters")
utt <- utt %>% filter(!corpus_name %in% EXCLUDE_CORPORA)

cat("Rows:", nrow(utt), "\n")
cat("Transcripts:", n_distinct(utt$transcript_id), "\n")
cat("Children:", n_distinct(utt$target_child_id), "\n")
cat("Corpora:", n_distinct(utt$corpus_name), "\n")
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 2. Select relevant columns

```{r select-cols}
crqa_all <- utt %>%
  dplyr::select(
    id,
    target_child_id,
    transcript_id,
    role_category,
    target_child_age,
    target_child_sex,
    emotion_count
  )
saveRDS(crqa_all, here("01Data", "02Derived", "CRQA Roles Sep.rds"))
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 3. Aggregate utterances → turns

```{r build-turns}
library(data.table)

# Keep only columns needed for CRQA
crqa_dt <- as.data.table(crqa_all)[, .(
  transcript_id,
  id,
  target_child_id,
  target_child_age,
  target_child_sex,
  role_category,
  emotion_count
)]

# Sort utterances chronologically within transcripts
setorder(crqa_dt, transcript_id, id)

# Identify speaker category
crqa_dt[, speaker_category := fifelse(
  role_category == "Target Child",
  "child",
  "partner"
)]

# Identify changes between child and partner
crqa_dt[, turn_id := rleid(speaker_category),
        by = transcript_id]

# Aggregate utterances into conversational turns
crqa_turns <- crqa_dt[, .(
  target_child_id  = first(target_child_id),
  target_child_age = first(target_child_age),
  target_child_sex = first(target_child_sex),
  speaker_category = first(speaker_category),
  emotion_count    = sum(emotion_count, na.rm = TRUE),
  n_utts           = .N
), by = .(transcript_id, turn_id)]

# Sort final output
setorder(crqa_turns, transcript_id, turn_id)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 3b. Enforce partner-first alignment

```{r partner-first}
crqa_turns_pf <- crqa_turns %>%
  group_by(transcript_id) %>%
  arrange(turn_id, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
  filter(turn_id >= min(turn_id[speaker_category == "partner"])) %>%
  ungroup()

cat("Turns dropped:", nrow(crqa_turns) - nrow(crqa_turns_pf), "\n")
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 4. Build separate binary series per speaker

```{r build-series}
crqa_series <- crqa_turns_pf %>%
  mutate(has_emotion = as.integer(emotion_count > 0)) %>%
  group_by(transcript_id) %>%
  summarise(
    target_child_id  = first(target_child_id),
    target_child_age = first(target_child_age),
    target_child_sex = first(target_child_sex),
    child_series     = list(has_emotion[speaker_category == "child"]),
    partner_series   = list(has_emotion[speaker_category == "partner"]),
    n_child_turns    = sum(speaker_category == "child"),
    n_partner_turns  = sum(speaker_category == "partner"),
    child_emo_rate   = mean(has_emotion[speaker_category == "child"]),
    partner_emo_rate = mean(has_emotion[speaker_category == "partner"]),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(n_aligned = pmin(n_child_turns, n_partner_turns))

saveRDS(crqa_series, here("01Data", "02Derived", "CRQA full data.rds"))
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 5. Choose window size W from inter-event intervals

Because emotion words are rare, the window W should reflect the typical spacing *between* emotional expressions — not the duration of an emotion episode. If coupling exists, a partner's responsive emotion word should arrive within the next inter-event interval of the child's signal (and vice versa). Setting W to the median IEI ensures the diagonal band is wide enough to capture most genuine coupled pairs, without extending so far that random co-occurrence dominates.

An inter-event interval (IEI) is the gap in turns between two consecutive emotion words in the same series.

```{r choose-window}
compute_iei <- function(series) {
  positions <- which(series == 1L)
  if (length(positions) < 2) return(integer(0))
  diff(positions)
}

all_iei <- crqa_series %>%
  pmap(function(child_series, partner_series, ...) {
    c(compute_iei(unlist(child_series)),
      compute_iei(unlist(partner_series)))
  }) %>%
  unlist()

iei_summary <- tibble(
  mean   = mean(all_iei),
  median = median(all_iei),
  sd     = sd(all_iei),
  p25    = quantile(all_iei, 0.25),
  p75    = quantile(all_iei, 0.75)
)

cat("Inter-event interval (turns between consecutive emotion words):\n")
print(round(iei_summary, 2))

# W = ceiling of median IEI
WINDOW_W <- ceiling(median(all_iei))
cat(sprintf("\nChosen window W: %d turns\n", WINDOW_W))

ggplot(tibble(iei = all_iei), aes(x = iei)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = WINDOW_W, colour = "red",
             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = WINDOW_W + 0.5, y = Inf, vjust = 1.5, hjust = 0,
           label = paste0("W = ", WINDOW_W), colour = "red", size = 3.5) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, quantile(all_iei, 0.95))) +
  labs(
    title    = "Distribution of inter-event intervals (emotion words)",
    subtitle = "Red line = chosen window W (ceiling of median IEI)",
    x = "Turns between consecutive emotion words", y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 6. Filter transcripts

Retain only transcripts where the aligned series length exceeds W — the minimum needed for the diagonal band to contain any cells.

```{r filter}
crqa_series_f <- crqa_series %>% filter(n_aligned > WINDOW_W)

cat(sprintf("Retained: %d  |  Excluded: %d\n",
            nrow(crqa_series_f),
            nrow(crqa_series) - nrow(crqa_series_f)))

#get final demo data for RQ2a 3a

crqa_series_f %>%
  distinct(target_child_id, target_child_sex) %>%
  count(target_child_sex)

crqa_series_f %>%
  summarise(
    n_transcripts = n_distinct(transcript_id),
    n_children    = n_distinct(target_child_id)
  )

crqa_series_f %>%
  summarise(
    min_age_months = min(target_child_age, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_age_months = max(target_child_age, na.rm = TRUE),
    min_age_years  = min(target_child_age, na.rm = TRUE) / 12,
    max_age_years  = max(target_child_age, na.rm = TRUE) / 12
  )
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 7. Cross-recurrence functions

We never build the full N×N matrix. Instead, we iterate over lags L from −W to +W and compute co-occurrence directly at each lag — equivalent to reading off each diagonal of the recurrence plot.

At lag L = j − i: - L ≥ 0: child\[1:(N−L)\] vs partner\[(L+1):N\] - L \< 0: child\[(\|L\|+1):N\] vs partner\[1:(N−\|L\|)\]

```{r crqa-functions}
# Co-occurrence count and cell count at a single lag
co_at_lag <- function(cs, ps, L) {
  N <- length(cs)
  if (L >= 0) {
    n_pairs <- N - L
    if (n_pairs <= 0) return(c(co = 0L, n = 0L))
    co <- sum(cs[1:n_pairs] == 1L & ps[(L + 1):N] == 1L)
  } else {
    aL      <- abs(L)
    n_pairs <- N - aL
    if (n_pairs <= 0) return(c(co = 0L, n = 0L))
    co <- sum(cs[(aL + 1):N] == 1L & ps[1:n_pairs] == 1L)
  }
  c(co = co, n = n_pairs)
}

# Full diagonal-band recurrence profile for lags -W..+W
recurrence_profile <- function(cs, ps, W) {
  N   <- min(length(cs), length(ps))
  cs  <- cs[1:N]; ps <- ps[1:N]
  lags <- seq(-W, W)
  map_dfr(lags, function(L) {
    r <- co_at_lag(cs, ps, L)
    tibble(lag = L, co = r["co"], n_cells = r["n"])
  })
}

# Summary metrics from profile
summarise_crqa <- function(profile, W = 4) {
  wRR <- sum(profile$co) / sum(profile$n_cells)
  
  pos <- profile %>% filter(lag >= 1,        lag <= W)      # +1 to +W
  neg <- profile %>% filter(lag >= -(W - 1), lag <= 0)      # 0 to -(W-1)
  
  RR_pos <- sum(pos$co) / sum(pos$n_cells)
  RR_neg <- sum(neg$co) / sum(neg$n_cells)
  
  tibble(wRR = wRR, RR_pos = RR_pos, RR_neg = RR_neg,
         asymmetry = RR_pos - RR_neg)
}
  
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 8. Compute observed wRR and asymmetry

```{r compute-observed}
crqa_results <- map_dfr(seq_len(nrow(crqa_series_f)), function(i) {
  cs <- unlist(crqa_series_f$child_series[[i]])
  ps <- unlist(crqa_series_f$partner_series[[i]])
  na <- crqa_series_f$n_aligned[i]

  prof <- recurrence_profile(cs[1:na], ps[1:na], W = WINDOW_W)
  summarise_crqa(prof) %>%
    mutate(
      transcript_id    = crqa_series_f$transcript_id[i],
      target_child_id  = crqa_series_f$target_child_id[i],
      target_child_age = crqa_series_f$target_child_age[i],
      target_child_sex = crqa_series_f$target_child_sex[i]
    )
})

cat("Observed wRR — mean:", round(mean(crqa_results$wRR), 5), "\n")
cat("Mean asymmetry:     ", round(mean(crqa_results$asymmetry), 5),
    "(+ = child leads)\n")
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 9. Shuffled baseline

Shuffle the child series to destroy temporal order while preserving its emission rate. Any remaining recurrence is due purely to base rates (both speakers happen to use emotion words at similar rates), not coupling. Subtracting this baseline removes the base-rate contribution from both wRR and asymmetry.

```{r shuffled-baseline}
crqa_results <- crqa_results %>%
  mutate(transcript_id = as.character(transcript_id))

crqa_series_f <- crqa_series_f %>%
  mutate(transcript_id = as.character(transcript_id))

utt <- utt %>%
  mutate(transcript_id = as.character(transcript_id))

set.seed(42)

crqa_shuffled <- map_dfr(seq_len(nrow(crqa_series_f)), function(i) {
  cs_shuf <- sample(unlist(crqa_series_f$child_series[[i]]))
  ps      <- unlist(crqa_series_f$partner_series[[i]])
  na      <- crqa_series_f$n_aligned[i]

  prof <- recurrence_profile(cs_shuf[1:na], ps[1:na], W = WINDOW_W)
  summarise_crqa(prof) %>%
    rename(wRR_shuf = wRR, RR_pos_shuf = RR_pos,
           RR_neg_shuf = RR_neg, asymmetry_shuf = asymmetry) %>%
    mutate(transcript_id = crqa_series_f$transcript_id[i])
})

# age_lookup built here for use in both the full-sample and dyadic pipelines
age_lookup <- utt %>%
  filter(role_category == "Target Child", !is.na(target_child_age)) %>%
  group_by(transcript_id) %>%
  summarise(
    target_child_age = first(target_child_age),
    target_child_sex = first(target_child_sex),
    target_child_id  = first(target_child_id),
    corpus_name      = first(corpus_name),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

crqa_data <- crqa_results %>%
  left_join(crqa_shuffled, by = "transcript_id") %>%
  dplyr::select(-target_child_age, -target_child_sex, -target_child_id) %>%
  left_join(age_lookup, by = "transcript_id") %>%
  left_join(
    crqa_series_f %>% dplyr::select(transcript_id, child_emo_rate, partner_emo_rate),
    by = "transcript_id"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    wRR_excess           = wRR - wRR_shuf,
    asymmetry_corrected  = (RR_pos - RR_pos_shuf) - (RR_neg - RR_neg_shuf),
    target_child_age_yrs = target_child_age / 12
  )

cat("Mean wRR (observed):       ", round(mean(crqa_data$wRR),        5), "\n")
cat("Mean wRR (shuffled):       ", round(mean(crqa_data$wRR_shuf),   5), "\n")
cat("Mean wRR excess:           ", round(mean(crqa_data$wRR_excess), 5), "\n")
cat("Mean corrected asymmetry:  ", round(mean(crqa_data$asymmetry_corrected), 5),
    "(+ = child leads)\n")
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 9.5. Reshape to long format

Both the RQ2 and RQ3 condition × age interaction models require data in long format, with one row per transcript × condition combination. The `(1 | transcript_id)` random effect in these models is the mixed-effects analogue of pairing: it absorbs stable transcript-level variance so that the condition contrast is identified from within-transcript variation only.

```{r reshape-long}
crqa_long_wrr <- crqa_data %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(wRR, wRR_shuf),
    names_to  = "condition",
    values_to = "wRR_value"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    condition = factor(
      if_else(condition == "wRR", "Observed", "Shuffled"),
      levels = c("Shuffled", "Observed")
    )
  )

crqa_long_asym <- crqa_data %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(asymmetry, asymmetry_shuf),
    names_to  = "condition",
    values_to = "asym_value"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    condition = factor(
      if_else(condition == "asymmetry", "Observed", "Shuffled"),
      levels = c("Shuffled", "Observed")
    )
  )

cat("Long-format rows (WRR):       ", nrow(crqa_long_wrr),  "\n")
cat("Long-format rows (Asymmetry): ", nrow(crqa_long_asym), "\n")
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## RQ2a. Temporal Contingency with the Social Environment Across Development

Across the full sample, children and their social partners showed systematic co-occurrence of emotion words across conversational turns. The analyses proceed in two parts. Part A characterises the aggregate cross-recurrence structure descriptively across all lags. Part B tests whether above-chance temporal coupling changes across child age.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### A. Aggregate Recurrence Profile

> **DESCRIPTIVE RESULT.** This section describes the mean recurrence structure across lags (−W to +W turns). No developmental inference is drawn here.

The cross-recurrence profile plots mean RR as a function of lag for observed and shuffled series. Concentration of recurrence near lag 0 indicates that emotion word co-occurrence is a short-range phenomenon; elevation above the shuffled baseline confirms that co-occurrence exceeds what is expected from independent base-rate contributions alone.

```{r agg-profile}
# Observed recurrence profile across all transcripts
profile_all <- map_dfr(seq_len(nrow(crqa_series_f)), function(i) {
  cs <- unlist(crqa_series_f$child_series[[i]])
  ps <- unlist(crqa_series_f$partner_series[[i]])
  na <- crqa_series_f$n_aligned[i]

  recurrence_profile(cs[1:na], ps[1:na], W = WINDOW_W) %>%
    mutate(
      RR            = co / n_cells,
      transcript_id = crqa_series_f$transcript_id[i]
    )
})

# Shuffled baseline profile (same seed as Section 9)
set.seed(42)
profile_shuf <- map_dfr(seq_len(nrow(crqa_series_f)), function(i) {
  cs_shuf <- sample(unlist(crqa_series_f$child_series[[i]]))
  ps      <- unlist(crqa_series_f$partner_series[[i]])
  na      <- crqa_series_f$n_aligned[i]

  recurrence_profile(cs_shuf[1:na], ps[1:na], W = WINDOW_W) %>%
    mutate(
      RR            = co / n_cells,
      transcript_id = crqa_series_f$transcript_id[i]
    )
})

# Summarise by lag across transcripts (function reused by partner profile below)
summarise_profile <- function(df, condition_label) {
  df %>%
    group_by(lag) %>%
    summarise(
      mean_RR = mean(RR, na.rm = TRUE),
      se_RR   = sd(RR,   na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n()),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    mutate(condition = condition_label)
}

profile_combined <- bind_rows(
  summarise_profile(profile_all,  "Observed"),
  summarise_profile(profile_shuf, "Shuffled")
)
```

```{r fig-rq2a-profile}
# Figure RQ2a-1. Aggregate cross-recurrence profile
ggplot(profile_combined, aes(x = lag, y = mean_RR,
                              colour = condition, fill = condition)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = mean_RR - se_RR, ymax = mean_RR + se_RR),
              alpha = 0.2, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Observed" = "#2980b9", "Shuffled" = "grey60")) +
  scale_fill_manual(  values = c("Observed" = "#2980b9", "Shuffled" = "grey60")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-WINDOW_W, WINDOW_W, by = 2)) +
  labs(
    title    = "Figure RQ2a-1. Mean cross-recurrence profile across all transcripts",
    subtitle = "Lag > 0: child leads  |  Lag ≤ 0: partner leads  |  shading = ±1 SE",
    x        = "Lag (turns)", y = "Mean RR",
    colour   = NULL, fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

*Reporting note (fill in after running):* The observed profile peaked at lag \[±X\] (mean RR = \[X\]), indicating that emotion word co-occurrence was most concentrated within \[X–X\] consecutive turns. Recurrence declined monotonically with increasing lag distance and converged toward the shuffled baseline at the window boundary (lag ±\[W\]). This profile pattern confirms that W = \[W\] turns captures the main concentration of temporal coupling without including lags at which observed and chance co-occurrence are indistinguishable.

*Lag asymmetry note:* \[If the profile is visibly asymmetric around lag 0, note whether positive or negative lags show higher RR — this prefigures the RQ3 asymmetry analysis.\]

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### B. Developmental Change in Temporal Contingency

> **INFERENTIAL RESULT.** This section tests whether above-chance temporal coupling — the gap between observed and shuffled WRR — changes with child age.

#### B.1. Overall above-chance temporal coupling

```{r rq2-test}
t.test(crqa_data$wRR, crqa_data$wRR_shuf,
       paired = TRUE, alternative = "greater")
```

#### B.2. Condition × Age Interaction Model (Primary Inferential Test)

The interaction model fits observed and shuffled WRR trajectories simultaneously. `(1 | transcript_id)` restores the paired structure: it absorbs stable transcript-level variance so the condition contrast is identified from within-transcript variation only — the mixed-effects analogue of a paired t-test.

*Reporting note:* Report the overall model (summary below), the omnibus LRT (B.3), and the predicted trajectory figure (B.7). Individual spline coefficients do not require narrative description.

```{r rq2-model}
m_rq2 <- lmer(
  wRR_value ~
    condition * ns(target_child_age_yrs, df = 3) +
    target_child_sex +
    (1 | corpus_name) +
    (1 | target_child_id) +
    (1 | transcript_id),
  data = crqa_long_wrr,
  REML = TRUE
)
summary(m_rq2)
confint(m_rq2, method = "Wald")
```

#### B.3. Omnibus Test — Does the Observed–Shuffled Gap Change Across Development?

A likelihood-ratio test on the 3-df interaction block tests whether the developmental trajectory of WRR differs between observed and shuffled conditions — i.e., whether the gap converges or diverges across age. This is the primary test of RQ2.

*Reporting note:* Report χ²(3), p. If significant, describe the developmental direction using emmeans (B.5) and the predicted trajectories (B.7). If non-significant, report that the gap was developmentally stable and cite the main effect of condition from B.2.

```{r rq2-lrt}
m_rq2_main <- lmer(
  wRR_value ~
    condition + ns(target_child_age_yrs, df = 3) +
    target_child_sex +
    (1 | corpus_name) + (1 | target_child_id) + (1 | transcript_id),
  data = crqa_long_wrr, REML = FALSE
)
m_rq2_inter <- lmer(
  wRR_value ~
    condition * ns(target_child_age_yrs, df = 3) +
    target_child_sex +
    (1 | corpus_name) + (1 | target_child_id) + (1 | transcript_id),
  data = crqa_long_wrr, REML = FALSE
)
anova(m_rq2_main, m_rq2_inter)
```

#### B.4. Supplementary — Difference Score Model

> **SUPPLEMENTARY.** The difference score model is secondary to B.2–B.3 and included for completeness. The primary inferential framework is the condition × age interaction (B.2).

The difference score (`wRR_excess = wRR − wRR_shuf`) directly quantifies above-chance temporal coupling. Framing note: the excess approaching zero at older ages means coupling *increasingly resembles independent contributions*, not that recurrence has disappeared — overall WRR remains substantial.

```{r rq2-excess-model}
m_rq2_excess <- lmer(
  wRR_excess ~
    ns(target_child_age_yrs, df = 3) +
    target_child_sex +
    (1 | corpus_name) + (1 | target_child_id),
  data = crqa_data, REML = TRUE
)
summary(m_rq2_excess)
confint(m_rq2_excess, method = "Wald")

# LRT: does above-chance coupling change across development?
m_rq2_excess_null <- lmer(
  wRR_excess ~ 1 + target_child_sex +
    (1 | corpus_name) + (1 | target_child_id),
  data = crqa_data, REML = FALSE
)
m_rq2_excess_age <- lmer(
  wRR_excess ~ ns(target_child_age_yrs, df = 3) + target_child_sex +
    (1 | corpus_name) + (1 | target_child_id),
  data = crqa_data, REML = FALSE
)
anova(m_rq2_excess_null, m_rq2_excess_age)
```

#### B.5. Estimated Marginal Means at Key Ages

> **INFERENTIAL RESULT.** Estimated marginal means from `m_rq2` at representative ages (2, 4, 6, 8, 10 years) quantify the observed vs. shuffled gap on the original scale and provide the key numbers for Results reporting.

*Reporting note:* Use `pairs(emmeans_rq2)` output to report the observed–shuffled contrast at each age. Describe the direction and magnitude of the gap at early vs. later ages to characterise the developmental trajectory in plain language.

```{r rq2-emmeans}
emmeans_rq2 <- emmeans(m_rq2,
                       ~ condition | target_child_age_yrs,
                       at = list(target_child_age_yrs = c(2, 4, 6, 8, 10)))
print(emmeans_rq2)
pairs(emmeans_rq2)
```

#### B.6. Distribution of Observed WRR

```{r rq2-dist-plot}
ggplot(crqa_data, aes(x = wRR)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(crqa_data$wRR_shuf, na.rm = TRUE),
             colour = "red", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text",
           x = mean(crqa_data$wRR_shuf, na.rm = TRUE) + 0.0002,
           y = Inf, vjust = 1.5, hjust = 0,
           label = "shuffled mean", colour = "red", size = 3.5) +
  labs(
    title    = "Distribution of windowed recurrence rate (wRR)",
    subtitle = paste0("Diagonal band ±", WINDOW_W, " turns  |  (1,1) recurrences only"),
    x = "wRR per transcript", y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

#### B.7. Model-Predicted Developmental Trajectories (Figure RQ2a-2)

> **INFERENTIAL RESULT.** Predicted WRR for observed and shuffled conditions from `m_rq2`, with 95% CI bands. This is the primary figure for RQ2a.

*Reporting note:* Describe the trajectory in terms of (1) whether observed WRR remains above shuffled across all ages (main effect of condition), and (2) whether the gap narrows, widens, or remains constant across development (interaction). Avoid reporting individual spline coefficients in the narrative.

```{r rq2-age-plot}
pred_rq2 <- ggpredict(m_rq2,
                      terms = c("target_child_age_yrs [all]", "condition"))

ggplot(as.data.frame(pred_rq2),
       aes(x = x, y = predicted, colour = group, fill = group,
           linetype = group)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high),
              alpha = 0.15, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.5) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("Observed" = "solid", "Shuffled" = "dotted")) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Observed" = "#2980b9", "Shuffled" = "grey60")) +
  scale_fill_manual(  values = c("Observed" = "#2980b9", "Shuffled" = "grey60")) +
  labs(
    title    = "Emotion Word Recurrence by Child Age",
    subtitle = "Model-estimated trajectories  |  shading = 95% CI",
    x        = "Child Age (Years)",
    y        = "Windowed Recurrence Rate",
    colour   = NULL, fill = NULL, linetype = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 18) +
  theme(
    legend.position  = "top",
    plot.title       = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```

#### B.8. Post-hoc — Child–Partner Emotion-Word Rate Correlation

> **DESCRIPTIVE RESULT.** This is a post-hoc association check, not a primary hypothesis test. It establishes whether the above-chance WRR could be partially explained by matching emission rates rather than genuine temporal coupling.

Are children who use more emotion words paired with partners who also use more? A Pearson correlation between per-transcript child and partner emotion-word rates quantifies this association.

```{r emo-rate-correlation}
# ── Pearson correlation: child vs. partner emotion-word rate ──────────────────
cor_result <- cor.test(crqa_data$child_emo_rate,
                       crqa_data$partner_emo_rate,
                       method = "pearson")

cat(sprintf(
  "r = %.2f, 95%% CI [%.2f, %.2f], t(%d) = %.2f, p %s\n",
  cor_result$estimate,
  cor_result$conf.int[1],
  cor_result$conf.int[2],
  cor_result$parameter,
  cor_result$statistic,
  ifelse(cor_result$p.value < .001, "< .001",
         sprintf("= %.3f", cor_result$p.value))
))
```

```{r emo-rate-scatter}
ggplot(crqa_data, aes(x = partner_emo_rate, y = child_emo_rate)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25, size = 1.2, colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "firebrick", linewidth = 1,
              fill = "firebrick", alpha = 0.15) +
  annotate("text",
           x = Inf, y = Inf, hjust = 1.1, vjust = 1.8,
           label = sprintf("r = %.2f, p < .001", cor_result$estimate),
           size = 4.5, fontface = "italic") +
  labs(
    title = "Child vs. Partner Emotion-Word Rate",
    x     = "Partner Emotion-Word Rate (proportion of turns)",
    y     = "Child Emotion-Word Rate (proportion of turns)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    plot.title       = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```

## RQ3a. Directionality with the Social Environment Across Development

The recurrence structure has been characterised in RQ2a. The analyses below test whether emotion word co-occurrence is directionally asymmetric — i.e., whether child-initiated sequences (child leads partner) are more or less frequent than partner-initiated sequences (partner leads child) — and whether the direction or magnitude of this asymmetry changes across development.

The Asymmetry Index (AI = RR at positive lags − RR at negative lags) quantifies directional bias: positive values indicate child leads; negative values indicate partner leads; zero indicates symmetric co-occurrence. The shuffled AI is theoretically ≈ 0 (shuffling destroys temporal order), so the observed–shuffled contrast isolates genuine directional bias from base-rate effects.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### A. Overall Directional Bias Above Chance

> **INFERENTIAL RESULT.** Overall paired comparison of observed vs. shuffled AI across the full sample.

```{r rq3-test}
# Overall paired test: observed asymmetry vs. shuffled asymmetry
# Directly compares the observed AI (RR_pos − RR_neg on real data) against the
# shuffled AI (same formula applied to shuffled series), avoiding reliance on
# the "corrected" difference metric.
t.test(crqa_data$asymmetry, crqa_data$asymmetry_shuf,
       paired = TRUE)
# Note: two-sided because we have no directional prediction about the overall
# sample; use alternative = "greater" if theory predicts child leads on average.
```

### B. Condition × Age Interaction Model (Primary Inferential Test)

> **INFERENTIAL RESULT.** The same interaction model structure applied to the Asymmetry Index. `conditionObserved` estimates directional bias above chance. The condition × age interaction tests whether the direction or magnitude of the leader–follower asymmetry changes across development.

*Reporting note:* Report `conditionObserved` coefficient (directional bias averaged over development) and the LRT in C. Describe the result in terms of which partner role (child or partner) leads, not in terms of spline coefficients.

```{r rq3-model}
m_rq3 <- lmer(
  asym_value ~
    condition * ns(target_child_age_yrs, df = 3) +
    target_child_sex +
    (1 | corpus_name) +
    (1 | target_child_id) +
    (1 | transcript_id),
  data = crqa_long_asym,
  REML = TRUE
)
summary(m_rq3)
confint(m_rq3, method = "Wald")

# Manipulation check: is shuffled AI indistinguishable from zero across age?
m_shuf_ai <- lmer(
  asym_value ~ ns(target_child_age_yrs, df = 3) +
    (1 | corpus_name) + (1 | target_child_id),
  data   = dplyr::filter(crqa_long_asym, condition == "Shuffled"),
  REML   = TRUE
)
confint(m_shuf_ai, method = "Wald")
```

### C. Omnibus Test — Does Directional Bias Change Across Development?

> **INFERENTIAL RESULT.** Primary test for RQ3. A 3-df likelihood-ratio test on the interaction block tests whether the AI trajectory differs between observed and shuffled conditions — i.e., whether directional bias changes across age.

*Reporting note:* Report χ²(3), p. If significant, use emmeans (D) and the trajectory figure (F) to describe the developmental change. If non-significant, report that directional bias was developmentally stable and cite the overall bias from section A.

```{r rq3-lrt}
m_rq3_main <- lmer(
  asym_value ~
    condition + ns(target_child_age_yrs, df = 3) +
    target_child_sex +
    (1 | corpus_name) + (1 | target_child_id) + (1 | transcript_id),
  data = crqa_long_asym, REML = FALSE
)
m_rq3_inter <- lmer(
  asym_value ~
    condition * ns(target_child_age_yrs, df = 3) +
    target_child_sex +
    (1 | corpus_name) + (1 | target_child_id) + (1 | transcript_id),
  data = crqa_long_asym, REML = FALSE
)
anova(m_rq3_main, m_rq3_inter)
```

### D. Estimated Marginal Means at Key Ages

> **INFERENTIAL RESULT.** Observed vs. shuffled AI at representative ages (2, 4, 6, 8, 10 years). Use `pairs(emmeans_rq3)` to report the directional contrast at each age.

```{r rq3-emmeans}
emmeans_rq3 <- emmeans(m_rq3,
                       ~ condition | target_child_age_yrs,
                       at = list(target_child_age_yrs = c(2, 4, 6, 8, 10)))
print(emmeans_rq3)
pairs(emmeans_rq3)
```

### E. Supplementary — Difference Score Model (RQ3)

> **SUPPLEMENTARY.** Secondary to B–D. The corrected asymmetry (`asymmetry_corrected`) directly quantifies above-chance directional bias. Since the shuffled AI ≈ 0, this is nearly equivalent to the raw observed AI but removes any residual base-rate contribution.

```{r rq3-excess-model}
m_rq3_corrected <- lmer(
  asymmetry_corrected ~
    ns(target_child_age_yrs, df = 3) +
    target_child_sex +
    (1 | corpus_name) + (1 | target_child_id),
  data = crqa_data, REML = TRUE
)
summary(m_rq3_corrected)
confint(m_rq3_corrected, method = "Wald")

# LRT: does above-chance directional bias change across development?
m_rq3_corr_null <- lmer(
  asymmetry_corrected ~ 1 + target_child_sex +
    (1 | corpus_name) + (1 | target_child_id),
  data = crqa_data, REML = FALSE
)
m_rq3_corr_age <- lmer(
  asymmetry_corrected ~ ns(target_child_age_yrs, df = 3) + target_child_sex +
    (1 | corpus_name) + (1 | target_child_id),
  data = crqa_data, REML = FALSE
)
anova(m_rq3_corr_null, m_rq3_corr_age)
```

### F-prelim. Note on Recurrence Profile

> The aggregate cross-recurrence profile (observed vs. shuffled across lags −W to +W) was characterised in **RQ2a, Section A** (Figure RQ2a-1). The profile objects `profile_all`, `profile_shuf`, and `profile_combined` were computed there and are available for use here. Visual asymmetry around lag 0 in Figure RQ2a-1 motivates the Asymmetry Index analyses below.
>
> The directional profile for each partner type is shown in **RQ3b, Section A** (Figure RQ3b-1).

### F. Model-Predicted Developmental Trajectories (Figure RQ3a-1)

> **INFERENTIAL RESULT.** Predicted AI for observed and shuffled conditions from `m_rq3`, with 95% CI bands. This is the primary figure for RQ3a.

The shuffled curve is expected to remain near zero across all ages (manipulation check). Deviation of the observed curve from zero indicates directional bias above chance; the developmental shape of this deviation (constant, increasing, or decreasing) is the primary finding for RQ3.

```{r rq3-age-plot}
pred_rq3 <- ggpredict(m_rq3,
                      terms = c("target_child_age_yrs [all]", "condition"))

ggplot(as.data.frame(pred_rq3),
       aes(x = x, y = predicted, colour = group, fill = group,
           linetype = group)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high),
              alpha = 0.15, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("Observed" = "solid", "Shuffled" = "dotted")) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Observed" = "#2980b9", "Shuffled" = "grey60")) +
  scale_fill_manual(  values = c("Observed" = "#2980b9", "Shuffled" = "grey60")) +
  labs(
    title    = "Directional asymmetry by child age",
    subtitle = "Model-estimated trajectories  |  Positive = child leads  |  shading = 95% CI",
    x        = "Child age (years)",
    y        = "Asymmetry Index (RR_pos − RR_neg)",
    colour   = NULL, fill = NULL, linetype = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

```{r save}
saveRDS(profile_all,  here("01Data", "02Derived", "crqa_profile_long.rds"))
```

## 13. Identify dyadic transcripts (target child + exactly 1 partner type)

For the partner-category analysis we restrict to transcripts where the target child interacts with **one** social partner type only. Transcripts where multiple partner categories appear (e.g. mother *and* sibling both speak) are excluded because the partner series would be a mixture of signals and the category label would be ambiguous.

```{r dyadic-identify}
# Count distinct partner types per transcript (excluding target child)
dyadic_info <- crqa_all %>%
  filter(role_category != "Target Child") %>%
  group_by(transcript_id) %>%
  summarise(
    n_partner_types = n_distinct(role_category),
    partner_type    = if_else(n_distinct(role_category) == 1,
                              first(role_category), NA_character_),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Keep only purely dyadic transcripts
dyadic_ids <- dyadic_info %>% filter(n_partner_types == 1)

cat("Total transcripts in crqa_all:       ", n_distinct(crqa_all$transcript_id), "\n")
cat("Dyadic (exactly 1 partner type):     ", nrow(dyadic_ids), "\n")
cat("Excluded (multiple partner types):   ",
    n_distinct(crqa_all$transcript_id) - nrow(dyadic_ids), "\n\n")

# Transcript counts per partner category
partner_counts <- dyadic_ids %>%
  count(partner_type, name = "n_transcripts") %>%
  arrange(desc(n_transcripts))

cat("Transcripts per partner category:\n")
print(partner_counts)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 14. Set inclusion threshold; select eligible categories

Categories with very few dyadic transcripts cannot support reliable CRQA estimates or mixed-model fitting. We set a minimum of **20 transcripts** per category after all filtering steps; categories below this threshold are excluded.

```{r dyadic-threshold}
MIN_N <- 20

eligible_categories <- partner_counts %>%
  filter(n_transcripts >= MIN_N) %>%
  pull(partner_type)

cat("Categories retained (n_transcripts >=", MIN_N, "):\n")
print(eligible_categories)

cat("\nCategories excluded:\n")
print(partner_counts %>% filter(n_transcripts < MIN_N))

dyadic_ids_f <- dyadic_ids %>% filter(partner_type %in% eligible_categories)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 15. Rebuild CRQA series for dyadic transcripts

Re-run the full turn-building → partner-first alignment → binary-series pipeline on the dyadic-only subset. The window W and all CRQA functions from Sections 5 and 7 are reused unchanged so that results are directly comparable with the full-sample analysis.

```{r dyadic-series}
# Attach partner_type to utterance-level data
crqa_all_dyadic <- crqa_all %>%
  mutate(transcript_id = as.character(transcript_id)) %>%
  filter(transcript_id %in% as.character(dyadic_ids_f$transcript_id)) %>%
  left_join(
    dyadic_ids_f %>%
      mutate(transcript_id = as.character(transcript_id)) %>%
      select(transcript_id, partner_type),
    by = "transcript_id"
  )

# Turn building (same logic as Section 3)
crqa_turns_dyadic <- crqa_all_dyadic %>%
  group_by(transcript_id) %>%
  arrange(id, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(
    speaker_category = if_else(role_category == "Target Child", "child", "partner"),
    turn_change      = speaker_category != lag(speaker_category,
                                               default = first(speaker_category)),
    turn_id          = cumsum(turn_change) + 1L
  ) %>%
  group_by(transcript_id, turn_id) %>%
  summarise(
    target_child_id  = first(target_child_id),
    target_child_age = first(target_child_age),
    target_child_sex = first(target_child_sex),
    partner_type     = first(partner_type),
    speaker_category = first(speaker_category),
    emotion_count    = sum(emotion_count, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_utts           = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(transcript_id, turn_id)

# Partner-first alignment (same logic as Section 3b)
crqa_turns_dyadic_pf <- crqa_turns_dyadic %>%
  group_by(transcript_id) %>%
  arrange(turn_id, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
  filter(turn_id >= min(turn_id[speaker_category == "partner"])) %>%
  ungroup()

# Build binary series per transcript (same logic as Section 4)
crqa_series_dyadic <- crqa_turns_dyadic_pf %>%
  mutate(has_emotion = as.integer(emotion_count > 0)) %>%
  group_by(transcript_id) %>%
  summarise(
    target_child_id  = first(target_child_id),
    target_child_age = first(target_child_age),
    target_child_sex = first(target_child_sex),
    partner_type     = first(partner_type),
    child_series     = list(has_emotion[speaker_category == "child"]),
    partner_series   = list(has_emotion[speaker_category == "partner"]),
    n_child_turns    = sum(speaker_category == "child"),
    n_partner_turns  = sum(speaker_category == "partner"),
    child_emo_rate   = mean(has_emotion[speaker_category == "child"]),
    partner_emo_rate = mean(has_emotion[speaker_category == "partner"]),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(n_aligned = pmin(n_child_turns, n_partner_turns))

# Apply same minimum-length filter as Section 6
crqa_series_dyadic_f <- crqa_series_dyadic %>% filter(n_aligned > WINDOW_W)

cat(sprintf("Dyadic transcripts retained after length filter: %d  |  Excluded: %d\n",
            nrow(crqa_series_dyadic_f),
            nrow(crqa_series_dyadic) - nrow(crqa_series_dyadic_f)))

# Re-check counts per category after length filter; flag any that dropped below MIN_N
final_counts <- count(crqa_series_dyadic_f, partner_type, name = "n_final")
cat("\nFinal transcript counts per partner category:\n")
print(final_counts)

below_threshold <- final_counts %>% filter(n_final < MIN_N)
if (nrow(below_threshold) > 0) {
  cat("\nCategories dropped (fell below MIN_N after length filter):\n")
  print(below_threshold)
  crqa_series_dyadic_f <- crqa_series_dyadic_f %>%
    filter(partner_type %in% (final_counts %>% filter(n_final >= MIN_N) %>% pull(partner_type)))
  cat("Final retained categories:", unique(crqa_series_dyadic_f$partner_type), "\n")
}

# Fix target_child_age: first() in the turn summarise picks up partner rows where age
# is NA (CHILDES stores age only on child-speaker rows). Reuse age_lookup from Section 9.
crqa_series_dyadic_f <- crqa_series_dyadic_f %>%
  mutate(transcript_id = as.character(transcript_id)) %>%
  dplyr::select(-target_child_age, -target_child_sex, -target_child_id) %>%
  dplyr::left_join(
    age_lookup,
    by = "transcript_id"
  )

cat("\nNA in target_child_age after fix:", sum(is.na(crqa_series_dyadic_f$target_child_age)), "\n")
```

## 15b. Age coverage per partner category

```{r age-coverage}

# ── OVERALL: N children and transcripts in dyadic CRQA sample ─────────────

crqa_series_dyadic_f %>%
  summarise(
    n_transcripts = n(),
    n_children    = n_distinct(target_child_id)
  )

# ── BY PARTNER TYPE: N transcripts, N children, age range, sex ────────────

crqa_series_dyadic_f %>%

crqa_partner_demo <- crqa_series_dyadic_f %>%

    n_transcripts = n_distinct(transcript_id),

crqa_series_dyadic_f %>%

print(age_coverage)

# Visual: age distribution per partner type
ggplot(crqa_series_dyadic_f,
       aes(x = target_child_age / 12, y = partner_type, fill = partner_type)) +
  ggridges::geom_density_ridges(alpha = 0.6, scale = 0.9,
                                 quantile_lines = TRUE, quantiles = 2) +
  labs(
    title    = "Age distribution of transcripts by partner type",

    x = "Child age (years)", y = NULL
  ) +
```

## 16. Compute observed wRR and asymmetry per dyadic transcript

Uses the same `recurrence_profile()` and `summarise_crqa()` functions from Section 7 and the same global window W.

```{r dyadic-observed}
crqa_results_dyadic <- map_dfr(seq_len(nrow(crqa_series_dyadic_f)), function(i) {
  cs <- unlist(crqa_series_dyadic_f$child_series[[i]])
  ps <- unlist(crqa_series_dyadic_f$partner_series[[i]])
  na <- crqa_series_dyadic_f$n_aligned[i]

  recurrence_profile(cs[1:na], ps[1:na], W = WINDOW_W) %>%
    summarise_crqa() %>%
    mutate(
      transcript_id    = crqa_series_dyadic_f$transcript_id[i],
      target_child_id  = crqa_series_dyadic_f$target_child_id[i],
      target_child_age = crqa_series_dyadic_f$target_child_age[i],
      target_child_sex = crqa_series_dyadic_f$target_child_sex[i],
      partner_type     = crqa_series_dyadic_f$partner_type[i]
    )
})

# Shuffled baseline (same seed as Section 9 for reproducibility)
set.seed(42)
crqa_shuffled_dyadic <- map_dfr(seq_len(nrow(crqa_series_dyadic_f)), function(i) {
  cs_shuf <- sample(unlist(crqa_series_dyadic_f$child_series[[i]]))
  ps      <- unlist(crqa_series_dyadic_f$partner_series[[i]])
  na      <- crqa_series_dyadic_f$n_aligned[i]

  recurrence_profile(cs_shuf[1:na], ps[1:na], W = WINDOW_W) %>%
    summarise_crqa() %>%
    rename(wRR_shuf = wRR, RR_pos_shuf = RR_pos,
           RR_neg_shuf = RR_neg, asymmetry_shuf = asymmetry) %>%
    mutate(transcript_id = crqa_series_dyadic_f$transcript_id[i])
})

# Combine and compute excess / corrected asymmetry
# Re-join age_lookup to guarantee non-NA age (see fix in Section 15)
crqa_data_dyadic <- crqa_results_dyadic %>%
  mutate(transcript_id = as.character(transcript_id)) %>%
  left_join(
    crqa_shuffled_dyadic %>%
      mutate(transcript_id = as.character(transcript_id)),
    by = "transcript_id"
  ) %>%
  select(-target_child_age, -target_child_sex, -target_child_id) %>%
  left_join(age_lookup, by = "transcript_id") %>%
  mutate(
    wRR_excess = wRR - wRR_shuf,
    asymmetry_corrected = (RR_pos - RR_pos_shuf) -
      (RR_neg - RR_neg_shuf),
    target_child_age_yrs = target_child_age / 12,
    partner_type = factor(partner_type)
  )

cat("Dyadic CRQA data rows:", nrow(crqa_data_dyadic), "\n")
crqa_data_dyadic %>%
  group_by(partner_type) %>%
  summarise(
    n         = n(),
    mean_wRR  = round(mean(wRR),              4),
    mean_exc  = round(mean(wRR_excess),       4),
    mean_asym = round(mean(asymmetry_corrected), 4),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  print()
```

## RQ2b. Temporal Contingency Across Partner Types

```{r partner-colours}
# Shared colour palette — defined once, reused in every section-17 plot
partner_cols <- c(
  "Mother"      = "#57b403",
  "Father"      = "#a58aff",
  "Known Adult" = "#c59a00",
  "Other Adult" = "#06b6eb"
)
```

### A. Partner-Specific Recurrence Profile

> **DESCRIPTIVE RESULT.** The following section characterises mean recurrence across lags separately for each partner type. No developmental inference is drawn here.

```{r partner-profile}
# Compute observed recurrence profile per dyadic transcript
profile_partner_obs <- map_dfr(seq_len(nrow(crqa_series_dyadic_f)), function(i) {
  cs <- unlist(crqa_series_dyadic_f$child_series[[i]])
  ps <- unlist(crqa_series_dyadic_f$partner_series[[i]])
  na <- crqa_series_dyadic_f$n_aligned[i]

  recurrence_profile(cs[1:na], ps[1:na], W = WINDOW_W) %>%
    mutate(
      RR           = co / n_cells,
      transcript_id = crqa_series_dyadic_f$transcript_id[i],
      partner_type  = crqa_series_dyadic_f$partner_type[i]
    )
})

# Shuffled baseline per dyadic transcript (same seed)
set.seed(42)
profile_partner_shuf <- map_dfr(seq_len(nrow(crqa_series_dyadic_f)), function(i) {
  cs_shuf <- sample(unlist(crqa_series_dyadic_f$child_series[[i]]))
  ps      <- unlist(crqa_series_dyadic_f$partner_series[[i]])
  na      <- crqa_series_dyadic_f$n_aligned[i]

  recurrence_profile(cs_shuf[1:na], ps[1:na], W = WINDOW_W) %>%
    mutate(
      RR            = co / n_cells,
      transcript_id = crqa_series_dyadic_f$transcript_id[i],
      partner_type  = crqa_series_dyadic_f$partner_type[i]
    )
})

# Summarise by partner type and lag
profile_partner_combined <- bind_rows(
  profile_partner_obs %>%
    group_by(partner_type, lag) %>%
    summarise(mean_RR = mean(RR, na.rm = TRUE),
              se_RR   = sd(RR,   na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n()),
              .groups = "drop") %>%
    mutate(condition = "Observed"),
  profile_partner_shuf %>%
    group_by(partner_type, lag) %>%
    summarise(mean_RR = mean(RR, na.rm = TRUE),
              se_RR   = sd(RR,   na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n()),
              .groups = "drop") %>%
    mutate(condition = "Shuffled")
)

# Peak RR per partner type (observed only)
profile_partner_obs %>%
  group_by(partner_type, lag) %>%
  summarise(mean_RR = mean(RR, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(partner_type) %>%
  slice_max(mean_RR, n = 1) %>%
  arrange(desc(mean_RR))
```

```{r fig-rq2b-profile}
# Figure RQ2b-1. Partner-specific cross-recurrence profile
ggplot(profile_partner_combined,
       aes(x = lag, y = mean_RR, colour = condition, fill = condition)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = mean_RR - se_RR, ymax = mean_RR + se_RR),
              alpha = 0.2, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  facet_wrap(~ partner_type, ncol = 2, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Observed" = "#2980b9", "Shuffled" = "grey60")) +
  scale_fill_manual(  values = c("Observed" = "#2980b9", "Shuffled" = "grey60")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-WINDOW_W, WINDOW_W, by = 2)) +
  labs(
    title    = "Figure RQ2b-1. Cross-recurrence profile by partner type",
    subtitle = "Lag > 0: child leads  |  Lag ≤ 0: partner leads  |  shading = ±1 SE",
    x        = "Lag (turns)", y = "Mean RR",
    colour   = NULL, fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top",
        strip.text      = element_text(face = "bold"))
```

### B. Developmental Trajectories by Partner Type

> **INFERENTIAL RESULT.** Mixed-effects models test whether WRR developmental trajectories differ across partner types, and whether the partner-specific observed–shuffled gap changes across age.

#### B.1. Long-format dyadic data (observed + shuffled)

```{r dyadic-long-wrr}
crqa_dyadic_long_wrr <- crqa_data_dyadic %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(wRR, wRR_shuf),
    names_to  = "condition",
    values_to = "wRR_value"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    condition = factor(
      if_else(condition == "wRR", "Observed", "Shuffled"),
      levels = c("Shuffled", "Observed")
    )
  )

cat("Dyadic long-format rows (WRR):", nrow(crqa_dyadic_long_wrr), "\n")
```

#### B.2. Three-way model — partner type × condition × age

This model tests: (a) whether partner types differ in observed WRR trajectory (partner_type × age); (b) whether above-chance coupling differs across partner types (partner_type × condition); (c) whether the developmental trajectory of above-chance coupling differs across partner types (partner_type × condition × age).

*Note: Father and Known Adult have limited sample sizes (see Section 15b). Models restricted to Mother vs. Other Adult (B.3) provide the cleanest test of trajectory differences.*

```{r rq2b-full-model}
crqa_dyadic_long_wrr <- crqa_dyadic_long_wrr %>%
  mutate(partner_type = relevel(factor(partner_type), ref = "Mother"))

m_rq2b_full <- lmer(
  wRR_value ~
    partner_type * condition * ns(target_child_age_yrs, df = 3) +
    target_child_sex +
    (1 | corpus_name) + (1 | target_child_id) + (1 | transcript_id),
  data = crqa_dyadic_long_wrr,
  REML = FALSE
)
# Note any convergence warnings
summary(m_rq2b_full)
```

```{r rq2b-lrt}
# LRT: does the partner × condition × age three-way interaction improve fit?
m_rq2b_twoway <- lmer(
  wRR_value ~
    (partner_type + condition + ns(target_child_age_yrs, df = 3))^2 +
    target_child_sex +
    (1 | corpus_name) + (1 | target_child_id) + (1 | transcript_id),
  data = crqa_dyadic_long_wrr,
  REML = FALSE
)
anova(m_rq2b_twoway, m_rq2b_full)
```

#### B.3. Restricted model — Mother vs. Other Adult

```{r rq2b-restricted}
crqa_mo_long <- crqa_dyadic_long_wrr %>%
  filter(partner_type %in% c("Mother", "Other Adult")) %>%
  mutate(partner_type = relevel(droplevels(partner_type), ref = "Mother"))

m_rq2b_mo <- lmer(
  wRR_value ~
    partner_type * condition * ns(target_child_age_yrs, df = 3) +
    target_child_sex +
    (1 | corpus_name) + (1 | target_child_id) + (1 | transcript_id),
  data = crqa_mo_long,
  REML = FALSE
)
summary(m_rq2b_mo)

# LRT: three-way vs. two-way
m_rq2b_mo_twoway <- lmer(
  wRR_value ~
    (partner_type + condition + ns(target_child_age_yrs, df = 3))^2 +
    target_child_sex +
    (1 | corpus_name) + (1 | target_child_id) + (1 | transcript_id),
  data = crqa_mo_long,
  REML = FALSE
)
anova(m_rq2b_mo_twoway, m_rq2b_mo)

# Refit with REML for final estimates
m_rq2b_mo_reml <- update(m_rq2b_mo, REML = TRUE)
confint(m_rq2b_mo_reml, method = "Wald")
```

```{r fig-rq2b-trajectories}
# Figure RQ2b-2. Partner-specific WRR trajectories (observed vs. shuffled)
ggpredict(m_rq2b_mo_reml,
          terms = c("target_child_age_yrs [all]", "condition", "partner_type")) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = predicted, colour = group, fill = group, linetype = group)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = 0.15, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~ facet, ncol = 2) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("Observed" = "solid", "Shuffled" = "dotted")) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Observed" = "#2980b9", "Shuffled" = "grey60")) +
  scale_fill_manual(  values = c("Observed" = "#2980b9", "Shuffled" = "grey60")) +
  labs(
    title    = "Figure RQ2b-2. WRR developmental trajectories by partner type",
    subtitle = "Model-estimated (Mother vs. Other Adult)  |  shading = 95% CI",
    x = "Child age (years)", y = "WRR",
    colour = NULL, fill = NULL, linetype = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))
```

### D. Supplementary — Observed-Only Partner × Age Model

> **SUPPLEMENTARY INFERENTIAL.** This model uses observed WRR only (no shuffled condition). It is supplementary to the condition × age interaction models in B.2–B.3, which are the primary inferential analyses for RQ2b.

`Mother` is used as the reference level. The model includes a `partner_type × age` interaction to test whether developmental trajectories differ across partner categories.

> **Interpretation note.** In an interaction model the `partner_type` main-effect coefficients are *intercept contrasts* at the natural spline's reference point (approximately the lower boundary of the age range), not average differences across the full developmental span. Non-significant interaction terms mean trajectory *shapes* do not differ significantly, even if the intercept contrast is significant.

```{r partner-wrr-model}
crqa_data_dyadic <- crqa_data_dyadic %>%
  mutate(partner_type = relevel(partner_type, ref = "Mother"))

m_partner_wrr <- lmer(
  wRR ~
    partner_type * ns(target_child_age_yrs, df = 3) +
    target_child_sex +
    (1 | corpus_name) +
    (1 | target_child_id),
  data = crqa_data_dyadic,
  REML = TRUE
)
summary(m_partner_wrr)

# LRT: is the interaction warranted?
anova(
  update(m_partner_wrr, . ~ partner_type + ns(target_child_age_yrs, df = 3) +
           target_child_sex + (1 | corpus_name) + (1 | target_child_id), REML = FALSE),
  update(m_partner_wrr, REML = FALSE)
)
```

```{r partner-wrr-model-plot, message=FALSE}
ggplot(
  ggeffects::ggpredict(m_partner_wrr,
                       terms = c("target_child_age_yrs [all]", "partner_type")) %>%
    as.data.frame(),
  aes(x = x, y = predicted, colour = group, fill = group)
) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = 0.15, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_line(
    data = crqa_data_dyadic %>%
      mutate(age_bin = round(target_child_age_yrs, 1)) %>%
      group_by(partner_type, age_bin) %>%
      summarise(mean_shuf = mean(wRR_shuf, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop"),
    mapping = aes(x = age_bin, y = mean_shuf, colour = partner_type),
    linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.6, inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(name = "Partner type", values = partner_cols) +
  scale_fill_manual(  name = "Partner type", values = partner_cols) +
  labs(
    title    = "Observed WRR (solid) vs. shuffled baseline (dashed) by partner type",
    subtitle = "Model-estimated trajectories  |  partner_type × age interaction  |  shading = 95% CI",
    x = "Child age (years)", y = "WRR"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

### E. Supplementary — Restricted Observed-Only Model (Mother vs. Other Adult)

Father (14 children) and Known Adult (4 children, 2–5.4 yr) have insufficient data to estimate a trajectory interaction reliably; Known Adult interaction terms are dropped by lmer due to rank deficiency. This model restricts to the two groups with adequate age coverage (Mother, Other Adult) to obtain an unconfounded test of trajectory difference.

```{r partner-wrr-restricted}
)

# LRT: interaction warranted?

           target_child_sex + (1 | corpus_name) + (1 | target_child_id), REML = FALSE),

)
```

## RQ3b. Directionality Across Partner Types

The recurrence profile for each partner type was characterised in RQ2b, Section A (Figure RQ2b-1). The directional asymmetry between the positive-lag and negative-lag sides of each profile indicates whether a given partner type tends to follow or lead the child's emotion words.

The analyses below test whether directional bias (Asymmetry Index) differs across partner types, and whether the developmental trajectory of directional bias differs by partner.

### A. Partner-Specific Directionality Profile

> **DESCRIPTIVE RESULT.** The lag profiles from Figure RQ2b-1 already show directional structure within each partner type. The table below quantifies mean AI and corrected AI (above-chance directional bias) per partner type.

```{r rq3b-descriptive}
crqa_data_dyadic %>%
  group_by(partner_type) %>%
  summarise(
    n               = n(),
    mean_AI_obs     = round(mean(asymmetry, na.rm = TRUE), 5),
    mean_AI_shuf    = round(mean(asymmetry_shuf, na.rm = TRUE), 5),
    mean_AI_corr    = round(mean(asymmetry_corrected, na.rm = TRUE), 5),
    sd_AI_corr      = round(sd(asymmetry_corrected, na.rm = TRUE), 5),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

*Reporting note (fill in after running):* For each partner type, note whether mean AI is positive (child leads) or negative (partner leads), and whether the corrected AI (above chance) is appreciably different from zero. Qualitative comparison across partner types motivates the inferential model below.

## 19. Sensitivity analysis — window size

To verify that findings are not an artefact of the window-size choice, the key RQ2 and RQ3 statistics are recomputed across candidate windows W − 2, W − 1, W (primary), W + 1, and W + 2. For each candidate W, the same length filter (`n_aligned > W`) is applied, so transcript counts may differ slightly. Results are considered robust if RQ2 remains significant (p \< .05) and the direction and approximate magnitude of the corrected asymmetry (RQ3) are stable across the range.

```{r sensitivity-window}
candidate_Ws <- (WINDOW_W - 2):(WINDOW_W + 2)
candidate_Ws <- candidate_Ws[candidate_Ws >= 1]   # W must be at least 1

set.seed(42)

sensitivity_results <- map_dfr(candidate_Ws, function(W_cand) {

  series_w <- crqa_series %>% filter(n_aligned > W_cand)

  obs <- map_dfr(seq_len(nrow(series_w)), function(i) {
    cs <- unlist(series_w$child_series[[i]])
    ps <- unlist(series_w$partner_series[[i]])
    na <- series_w$n_aligned[i]
    recurrence_profile(cs[1:na], ps[1:na], W = W_cand) %>% summarise_crqa()
  })

  shuf <- map_dfr(seq_len(nrow(series_w)), function(i) {
    cs_s <- sample(unlist(series_w$child_series[[i]]))
    ps   <- unlist(series_w$partner_series[[i]])
    na   <- series_w$n_aligned[i]
    recurrence_profile(cs_s[1:na], ps[1:na], W = W_cand) %>%
      summarise_crqa() %>%
      rename(wRR_shuf = wRR, asymmetry_shuf = asymmetry) %>%
      dplyr::select(wRR_shuf, asymmetry_shuf)
  })

  d   <- bind_cols(obs, shuf)
  rq2 <- t.test(d$wRR,       d$wRR_shuf,       paired = TRUE, alternative = "greater")
  rq3 <- t.test(d$asymmetry, d$asymmetry_shuf, paired = TRUE)

  tibble(
    W               = W_cand,
    primary         = (W_cand == WINDOW_W),
    n_transcripts   = nrow(d),
    mean_wRR_obs    = round(mean(d$wRR),                          5),
    mean_wRR_excess = round(mean(d$wRR - d$wRR_shuf),             5),
    rq2_t           = round(rq2$statistic,                        3),
    rq2_p           = round(rq2$p.value,                          4),
    mean_asym_obs   = round(mean(d$asymmetry),                    6),
    mean_asym_corr  = round(mean(d$asymmetry - d$asymmetry_shuf), 6),
    rq3_t           = round(rq3$statistic,                        3),
    rq3_p           = round(rq3$p.value,                          4)
  )
})

print(sensitivity_results)
```

`primary = TRUE` marks the window used in the main analysis (W = `r WINDOW_W` turns). Columns: `mean_wRR_excess` = mean observed minus shuffled wRR (RQ2 effect size); `mean_asym_corr` = mean corrected asymmetry index (RQ3 effect size).
